From parity checks to fault-tolerant machinesReview · 0 due

Module 1 · 80–100 minutes

Why more faulty qubits can mean fewer errors

Assumes: Dirac notation and tensor products of qubits · Pauli matrices and their commutation · binomial probabilities · the FEC threshold idea from classical coding

Requires: Start here · Enables: Independent application

By the end, you can
  • Compute the exact repetition-code logical error under independent bit flips, its small-error leading term, and its majority-decoding threshold.
  • Derive the three-qubit bit-flip code's syndrome table and show why parity measurements preserve encoded amplitudes.
  • Derive the probabilities and conditional states after a single-qubit X rotation and prove exact recovery in every possible branch.
  • Compute repetition-code suppression ratios, extract Λ from measured rates, and explain the effects of a threshold and an error floor.
  • Identify phase, measurement, and correlated errors that defeat this model and explain what a repair must change.
  1. 1.1 · Majority vote and the first threshold
  2. 1.2 · Why the quantum case looks impossible
  3. 1.3 · Parity, not value: the three-qubit bit-flip code
  4. 1.4 · Discretization: how measurement turns a continuum into a coin flip
  5. 1.5 · Scaling, Λ, and what Google measured
  6. 1.6 · When the measurement itself is wrong
  7. 1.7 · Reconstruct and transfer

We will follow one stored qubit through encoding, noise, measurement, and recovery. The aim is to understand how these steps protect an unknown state and where that protection fails. A natural break is after §1.4.

Google made a quantum memory larger by adding more qubits that could themselves fail. Across the three code sizes tested, each increase approximately halved the measured logical error per correction cycle. The reported suppression factor was Λ=2.14±0.02\Lambda=2.14\pm0.02Λ=2.14±0.02 Quantum error correction below the surface code threshold, PDF p. 1 Original source ↗ · DOI: 10.1038/s41586-024-08449-y. Why did adding more places for faults to occur make the stored information safer?

An error need not be a full flip, either. Imagine one physical qubit undergoing an XXX rotation by an unknown angle, say one degree. There are continuously many possible angles but only finitely many entries in a correction table. How could that table repair the state without learning the angle?

As an illustrative target, suppose physical parts fail once in a thousand and the logical qubit must fail only once in a billion. How can error correction bridge that gap, and what does it cost in qubits, time, and wiring? These targets are separate from the measured rates above.

§

1.1 · Majority vote and the first threshold

Adding bits creates more opportunities for flips. It also raises the number needed to overturn the majority. When each bit is more likely right than wrong, the second effect wins.

Encode a classical bit b∈{0,1}b\in\{0,1\}b∈{0,1} as ddd identical bits, with odd ddd to avoid ties. For this repetition code, ddd is also its distance: all ddd bits must flip to turn one codeword into the other. After one noisy round, a majority decoder returns the value held by most bits in the received word yyy. The Hamming weight wH(y)=∑k=1dykw_H(y)=\sum_{k=1}^d y_kwH​(y)=∑k=1d​yk​ counts its ones; 1[A]\mathbf1[A]1[A] is one when AAA holds and zero otherwise:

enc⁡(b)=(b,…,b),b^(y)=1 ⁣[wH(y)≥d+12].\operatorname{enc}(b)=(b,\ldots,b),\qquad \widehat b(y)=\mathbf1\!\left[w_H(y)\geq\frac{d+1}{2}\right].enc(b)=(b,…,b),b(y)=1[wH​(y)≥2d+1​].
(1.1)Definition

For now, only the stored bits can flip. Each flips independently with probability ppp per round; preparation, readout, and decoding are perfect. This is the code-capacity model. Each round starts from a fresh encoded word, and the majority rule stays fixed. Here ppp and pLp_LpL​ are probabilities per round; rotation angles, when they appear, are in radians.

Let pL(d,p)p_L(d,p)pL​(d,p) be the probability that this decoder returns the wrong bit in one round:

pL(d,p)=∑j=(d+1)/2d(dj)pj(1−p)d−j.p_L(d,p)=\sum_{j=(d+1)/2}^{d}\binom dj p^j(1-p)^{d-j}.pL​(d,p)=j=(d+1)/2∑d​(jd​)pj(1−p)d−j.
(1.2)

Independence assigns a particular set of jjj flips probability pj(1−p)d−jp^j(1-p)^{d-j}pj(1−p)d−j. The factor (1−p)d−j(1-p)^{d-j}(1−p)d−j requires the remaining bits to stay unchanged. There are (dj)=d!/[j!(d−j)!]\binom dj=d!/[j!(d-j)!](jd​)=d!/[j!(d−j)!] such sets. They are mutually exclusive, so

Pr⁡(J=j)=(dj)pj(1−p)d−j,Pr⁡(b^≠b)=Pr⁡(J≥m)=∑j=mdPr⁡(J=j).\Pr(J=j)=\binom dj p^j(1-p)^{d-j},\qquad \Pr(\widehat b\ne b)=\Pr(J\geq m)=\sum_{j=m}^d\Pr(J=j).Pr(J=j)=(jd​)pj(1−p)d−j,Pr(b=b)=Pr(J≥m)=j=m∑d​Pr(J=j).

For b=0b=0b=0, at least mmm flips create a majority of ones. For b=1b=1b=1, the same number creates a majority of zeros. The rate therefore does not depend on the stored bit. Useful checks are

pL(1,p)=p,pL(3,p)=(32)p2(1−p)+(33)p3=3p2−3p3+p3=3p2−2p3,pL(d,0)=0,pL(d,1)=1.\begin{aligned} p_L(1,p)&=p,\\ p_L(3,p)&=\binom32p^2(1-p)+\binom33p^3 =3p^2-3p^3+p^3=3p^2-2p^3,\\ p_L(d,0)&=0,\qquad p_L(d,1)=1. \end{aligned}pL​(1,p)pL​(3,p)pL​(d,0)​=p,=(23​)p2(1−p)+(33​)p3=3p2−3p3+p3=3p2−2p3,=0,pL​(d,1)=1.​

The terms are nonnegative and sum to at most (p+1−p)d=1(p+1-p)^d=1(p+1−p)d=1. For d≥3d\geq3d≥3, a single flip is harmless: failure requires several faults together.

The approximation is accurate when (d−m)p≪1(d-m)p\ll1(d−m)p≪1 and r≪1r\ll1r≪1; small ppp alone is insufficient when ddd grows. For d=1d=1d=1, the tail is empty and pL=pp_L=ppL​=p. At fixed distance, the smallest failing patterns dominate.

The coefficient counts the smallest failing patterns. The power of ppp counts the independent flips each requires. At sufficiently small ppp, requiring another flip matters more than having more vulnerable patterns.

Where do the distance curves meet?

For odd-distance repetition codes with independent flips and the fixed majority decoder, where is the common interior crossing of pL(d,p)p_L(d,p)pL​(d,p) with pL=pp_L=ppL​=p? Set aside the endpoints p=0,1p=0,1p=0,1.

The crossing is p=1/2p=1/2p=1/2. Pairing complementary error patterns proves it in Eq. (1.4). A threshold from another code, noise model, and decoder need not apply here. Adding bits cannot help a fixed majority when each bit is more likely wrong than right.

Your prediction

(1.4)

Pair every error pattern with its complement. For d=2m−1d=2m-1d=2m−1, replacing ppp by 1−p1-p1−p exchanges the probabilities of those patterns. Change the summation index to k=d−jk=d-jk=d−j:

At p=1/2p=1/2p=1/2 the left-hand side is pLp_LpL​ itself, so 2pL=12p_L=12pL​=1. Odd ddd rules out tied votes.

To find which side benefits from a larger code, add two bits and keep the same majority rule. If the original block has J=m−1J=m-1J=m−1 flips, failure is introduced only if both new bits flip. If J=mJ=mJ=m, failure is removed only if neither new bit flips. Other weights keep their verdict:

pL(d+2,p)−pL(d,p)=Pr⁡(J=m−1)p2−Pr⁡(J=m)(1−p)2=(dm−1)pm+1(1−p)m−(dm)pm(1−p)m+1=(dm)[p(1−p)]m(2p−1).\begin{aligned} p_L(d+2,p)-p_L(d,p) &=\Pr(J=m-1)p^2-\Pr(J=m)(1-p)^2\\ &=\binom d{m-1}p^{m+1}(1-p)^m-\binom dm p^m(1-p)^{m+1}\\ &=\binom dm[p(1-p)]^m(2p-1). \end{aligned}pL​(d+2,p)−pL​(d,p)​=Pr(J=m−1)p2−Pr(J=m)(1−p)2=(m−1d​)pm+1(1−p)m−(md​)pm(1−p)m+1=(md​)[p(1−p)]m(2p−1).​

We used (dm−1)=(dm)\binom d{m-1}=\binom dm(m−1d​)=(md​) for d=2m−1d=2m-1d=2m−1. The difference is negative below one half, zero at one half, and positive above one half. Iterating from d=1d=1d=1 compares every odd distance with the unprotected bit.

Optional: why failure tends to zero. For fixed p<1/2p<1/2p<1/2, the flip fraction J/dJ/dJ/d concentrates around ppp as the code grows. Its mean is ppp and its variance is p(1−p)/dp(1-p)/dp(1−p)/d. Failure requires that fraction to reach at least one half. Chebyshev's inequality gives

pL(d,p)≤Pr⁡ ⁣(∣Jd−p∣≥12−p)≤p(1−p)d (12−p)2⟶0(d→∞, p<12 fixed).p_L(d,p)\leq\Pr\!\left(\left|\frac Jd-p\right|\geq\frac12-p\right) \leq\frac{p(1-p)}{d\,(\tfrac12-p)^2}\longrightarrow0\qquad(d\to\infty,\ p<\tfrac12\ \text{fixed}).pL​(d,p)≤Pr(​dJ​−p​≥21​−p)≤d(21​−p)2p(1−p)​⟶0(d→∞, p<21​ fixed).

For fixed majority decoding, larger blocks help below p=1/2p=1/2p=1/2 and hurt above it. Quantum redundancy must achieve this without copying an unknown state.

§

1.2 · Why the quantum case looks impossible

Quantum protection must add redundancy without cloning an unknown state, detect faults without reading the stored value, and handle rotations whose angles vary continuously.

A device can copy the orthogonal labels ∣0⟩|0\rangle∣0⟩ and ∣1⟩|1\rangle∣1⟩. It cannot copy every unknown superposition. Suppose a unitary UUU with a fixed blank ∣0⟩|0\rangle∣0⟩ could map both ∣ϕ⟩∣0⟩|\phi\rangle|0\rangle∣ϕ⟩∣0⟩ to ∣ϕ⟩∣ϕ⟩|\phi\rangle|\phi\rangle∣ϕ⟩∣ϕ⟩ and ∣ψ⟩∣0⟩|\psi\rangle|0\rangle∣ψ⟩∣0⟩ to ∣ψ⟩∣ψ⟩|\psi\rangle|\psi\rangle∣ψ⟩∣ψ⟩. Preserving inner products would require

⟨ϕ∣ψ⟩=⟨ϕ∣ψ⟩2.\langle\phi|\psi\rangle=\langle\phi|\psi\rangle^2.⟨ϕ∣ψ⟩=⟨ϕ∣ψ⟩2.
(1.5)
Derivation · A copier cannot preserve arbitrary inner products

Compare the input overlap with the proposed output overlap. Unitarity preserves inner products, so for normalized blanks

(⟨ϕ∣⟨0∣)U†U(∣ψ⟩∣0⟩)=⟨ϕ∣ψ⟩⟨0∣0⟩=⟨ϕ∣ψ⟩,(⟨ϕ∣⟨ϕ∣)(∣ψ⟩∣ψ⟩)=⟨ϕ∣ψ⟩⟨ϕ∣ψ⟩.\begin{aligned} (\langle\phi|\langle0|)U^\dagger U(|\psi\rangle|0\rangle) &=\langle\phi|\psi\rangle\langle0|0\rangle=\langle\phi|\psi\rangle,\\ (\langle\phi|\langle\phi|)(|\psi\rangle|\psi\rangle) &=\langle\phi|\psi\rangle\langle\phi|\psi\rangle. \end{aligned}(⟨ϕ∣⟨0∣)U†U(∣ψ⟩∣0⟩)(⟨ϕ∣⟨ϕ∣)(∣ψ⟩∣ψ⟩)​=⟨ϕ∣ψ⟩⟨0∣0⟩=⟨ϕ∣ψ⟩,=⟨ϕ∣ψ⟩⟨ϕ∣ψ⟩.​

Write z=⟨ϕ∣ψ⟩z=\langle\phi|\psi\ranglez=⟨ϕ∣ψ⟩. With the phases written here, z=z2z=z^2z=z2 requires z=0z=0z=0 or z=1z=1z=1: the states are orthogonal or identical. Allowing arbitrary output phases changes the condition to ∣z∣=∣z∣2|z|=|z|^2∣z∣=∣z∣2, with the same conclusion for physical states. A universal copier would also need to copy distinct nonorthogonal states, which this condition forbids.

Apply the basis-state copier to a superposition:

U[(α∣0⟩+β∣1⟩)∣0⟩]=α∣00⟩+β∣11⟩≠α2∣00⟩+αβ(∣01⟩+∣10⟩)+β2∣11⟩.U[(\alpha|0\rangle+\beta|1\rangle)|0\rangle] =\alpha|00\rangle+\beta|11\rangle \ne\alpha^2|00\rangle+\alpha\beta(|01\rangle+|10\rangle)+\beta^2|11\rangle.U[(α∣0⟩+β∣1⟩)∣0⟩]=α∣00⟩+β∣11⟩=α2∣00⟩+αβ(∣01⟩+∣10⟩)+β2∣11⟩.

The proposed product on the right has cross terms that conflict with linearity. For either basis state, those terms vanish, so copying is consistent with the classical case.

A second obstacle is measurement disturbance. A ZZZ measurement of ∣ψ⟩=α∣0⟩+β∣1⟩|\psi\rangle=\alpha|0\rangle+\beta|1\rangle∣ψ⟩=α∣0⟩+β∣1⟩ reports +1+1+1 with probability ∣α∣2|\alpha|^2∣α∣2 and leaves ∣0⟩|0\rangle∣0⟩. It reports −1-1−1 with probability ∣β∣2|\beta|^2∣β∣2 and leaves ∣1⟩|1\rangle∣1⟩, up to global phase.

A density operator records the probabilities of later measurements. For this pure input it is ρ=∣ψ⟩⟨ψ∣\rho=|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|ρ=∣ψ⟩⟨ψ∣.

Its diagonal entries in the computational basis are the populations ∣α∣2|\alpha|^2∣α∣2 and ∣β∣2|\beta|^2∣β∣2. Ignoring the ZZZ-measurement outcome leaves those entries unchanged.

Its off-diagonal entries, αβ∗\alpha\beta^*αβ∗ and its complex conjugate, carry the coherence between the two basis states. Ignoring the measurement outcome removes these entries. The unknown relative phase of a superposition is then lost.

The third obstacle is a continuum of possible errors. Use the course convention Y=iXZY=iXZY=iXZ and define the angle of an XXX rotation in radians by

RX(θ)≡e−iθX/2.R_X(\theta)\equiv e^{-i\theta X/2}.RX​(θ)≡e−iθX/2.
(1.6)Definition

The rotation combines an unchanged part with an XXX-flipped part:

RX(θ)=cos⁡(θ/2)I−isin⁡(θ/2)X.R_X(\theta)=\cos(\theta/2)I-i\sin(\theta/2)X.RX​(θ)=cos(θ/2)I−isin(θ/2)X.
(1.7)
Derivation · Separate even and odd powers of the Pauli

Separate the even and odd powers in the convergent exponential series. Since X2=IX^2=IX2=I, the even powers are III and the odd powers are XXX:

e−iθX/2=∑n=0∞(−iθ/2)nXnn!=[∑r=0∞(−1)r(θ/2)2r(2r)!]I−i[∑r=0∞(−1)r(θ/2)2r+1(2r+1)!]X=cos⁡(θ/2)I−isin⁡(θ/2)X.\begin{aligned} e^{-i\theta X/2} &=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-i\theta/2)^nX^n}{n!}\\ &=\left[\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^r(\theta/2)^{2r}}{(2r)!}\right]I -i\left[\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^r(\theta/2)^{2r+1}}{(2r+1)!}\right]X\\ &=\cos(\theta/2)I-i\sin(\theta/2)X. \end{aligned}e−iθX/2​=n=0∑∞​n!(−iθ/2)nXn​=[r=0∑∞​(2r)!(−1)r(θ/2)2r​]I−i[r=0∑∞​(2r+1)!(−1)r(θ/2)2r+1​]X=cos(θ/2)I−isin(θ/2)X.​

At θ=0\theta=0θ=0 the operator is III; at θ=π\theta=\piθ=π it is −iX-iX−iX, a full flip up to global phase. The first-order term −iθX/2-i\theta X/2−iθX/2 checks the sign. Norm is conserved because (cI+isX)(cI−isX)=(c2+s2)I=I(cI+isX)(cI-isX)=(c^2+s^2)I=I(cI+isX)(cI−isX)=(c2+s2)I=I for real c=cos⁡(θ/2)c=\cos(\theta/2)c=cos(θ/2) and s=sin⁡(θ/2)s=\sin(\theta/2)s=sin(θ/2). The expansion holds for every angle; only the coefficients of the two fixed operators change.

There are continuously many angles but only finitely many measurement outcomes. Yet every XXX rotation combines the same two operators, III and XXX. If an encoding makes the unchanged and flipped parts give different parity outcomes, measurement can separate them without estimating the angle. §1.4 will carry out that projection.

A Bloch sphere represents a pure qubit state by a unit arrow. Its coordinate along each Pauli axis is the mean outcome of measuring that Pauli. The states ∣0⟩|0\rangle∣0⟩ and ∣1⟩|1\rangle∣1⟩ lie at the north and south poles. The rotation picture starts at ∣0⟩|0\rangle∣0⟩; an XXX rotation moves the arrow toward the negative-yyy direction and reaches ∣1⟩|1\rangle∣1⟩ at angle π\piπ.

The permitted copier

Why does Eq. (1.5) allow a device to copy ∣0⟩|0\rangle∣0⟩ and ∣1⟩|1\rangle∣1⟩ even though it forbids copying every unknown qubit?

Your answer

These obstacles rule out copying an unknown state and voting on measurements of its value. The next section instead stores the amplitudes in a joint state and measures agreement between neighboring qubits.

§

1.3 · Parity, not value: the three-qubit bit-flip code

Store the amplitudes in a joint state, then measure whether neighboring bits agree. These parities can reveal a single bit flip without revealing the logical value.

A controlled-NOT gate, or CNOT, flips its target qubit when its control is ∣1⟩|1\rangle∣1⟩ and leaves the target unchanged when its control is ∣0⟩|0\rangle∣0⟩. The arrow 1→21\to21→2 names qubit 1 as control and qubit 2 as target.

Prepare the input on qubit 1 and ∣0⟩|0\rangle∣0⟩ blanks on qubits 2 and 3. Apply CNOTs 1→21\to21→2 and 1→31\to31→3. The input basis states become the logical basis states ∣0L⟩|0_L\rangle∣0L​⟩ and ∣1L⟩|1_L\rangle∣1L​⟩, and linearity gives

∣0L⟩≡∣000⟩,∣1L⟩≡∣111⟩,∣ψL⟩≡α∣000⟩+β∣111⟩,∣α∣2+∣β∣2=1.|0_L\rangle\equiv|000\rangle,\quad |1_L\rangle\equiv|111\rangle,\quad |\psi_L\rangle\equiv\alpha|000\rangle+\beta|111\rangle,\quad |\alpha|^2+|\beta|^2=1.∣0L​⟩≡∣000⟩,∣1L​⟩≡∣111⟩,∣ψL​⟩≡α∣000⟩+β∣111⟩,∣α∣2+∣β∣2=1.
(1.8)Definition

Linearity preserves the amplitudes in this joint state, without creating independent copies.

Parity groups 000000 with 111111, and 010101 with 101010. Measuring parity distinguishes agreement from disagreement while preserving superpositions within either group.

An ancilla is an extra qubit used to collect a measurement result. For either neighboring pair, prepare an ancilla in ∣0⟩|0\rangle∣0⟩ and let each data qubit control a CNOT onto it. Equal bits flip the ancilla twice or not at all; unequal bits flip it once. Measure the ancilla after both gates. Separate data measurements would instead reveal the logical value.

The parity checks are stabilizers, operators whose +1+1+1 eigenspaces contain the code:

S1≡Z1Z2,S2≡Z2Z3.S_1\equiv Z_1Z_2,\qquad S_2\equiv Z_2Z_3.S1​≡Z1​Z2​,S2​≡Z2​Z3​.
(1.9)Definition

Both checks return +1+1+1 on either code state. We record +1+1+1 as bit 000 and −1-1−1 as bit 111. The ordered record (s1,s2)(s_1,s_2)(s1​,s2​) is the syndrome. Identity factors are omitted: Z1Z2Z_1Z_2Z1​Z2​ means Z⊗Z⊗IZ\otimes Z\otimes IZ⊗Z⊗I. Write supp⁡(Si)\operatorname{supp}(S_i)supp(Si​) for the qubits on which SiS_iSi​ acts nontrivially:

Si∣ψL⟩=∣ψL⟩,SiXk∣ψL⟩=(−1)1[k∈supp⁡(Si)]Xk∣ψL⟩.S_i|\psi_L\rangle=|\psi_L\rangle,\qquad S_iX_k|\psi_L\rangle=(-1)^{\mathbf1[k\in\operatorname{supp}(S_i)]}X_k|\psi_L\rangle.Si​∣ψL​⟩=∣ψL​⟩,Si​Xk​∣ψL​⟩=(−1)1[k∈supp(Si​)]Xk​∣ψL​⟩.
(1.10)
Derivation · Compute the anticommutation signs

Count signs using ZX=−XZZX=-XZZX=−XZ. Each check multiplies equal ZZZ eigenvalues, giving +1+1+1 on either code state and their superposition. Operators on different qubits commute. Moving XkX_kXk​ through SiS_iSi​ costs a minus sign only when kkk lies in that check's support:

S1X1=−X1S1,S1X2=−X2S1,S1X3=+X3S1,S2X1=+X1S2,S2X2=−X2S2,S2X3=−X3S2.\begin{array}{lll} S_1X_1=-X_1S_1,& S_1X_2=-X_2S_1,& S_1X_3=+X_3S_1,\\ S_2X_1=+X_1S_2,& S_2X_2=-X_2S_2,& S_2X_3=-X_3S_2. \end{array}S1​X1​=−X1​S1​,S2​X1​=+X1​S2​,​S1​X2​=−X2​S1​,S2​X2​=−X2​S2​,​S1​X3​=+X3​S1​,S2​X3​=−X3​S2​.​

Acting on the stabilized state removes the rightmost SiS_iSi​. For example,

X2∣ψL⟩=α∣010⟩+β∣101⟩,S1X2∣ψL⟩=−α∣010⟩−β∣101⟩,S2X2∣ψL⟩=−α∣010⟩−β∣101⟩.\begin{aligned} X_2|\psi_L\rangle&=\alpha|010\rangle+\beta|101\rangle,\\ S_1X_2|\psi_L\rangle&=-\alpha|010\rangle-\beta|101\rangle,\\ S_2X_2|\psi_L\rangle&=-\alpha|010\rangle-\beta|101\rangle. \end{aligned}X2​∣ψL​⟩S1​X2​∣ψL​⟩S2​X2​∣ψL​⟩​=α∣010⟩+β∣101⟩,=−α∣010⟩−β∣101⟩,=−α∣010⟩−β∣101⟩.​

Both logical components acquire the same check signs. Converting those signs to syndrome bits identifies parity without revealing the amplitudes.

If the middle qubit flips, the components become 010010010 and 101101101. Both neighboring pairs disagree in either component, so both give (1,1)(1,1)(1,1). The ancillas identify the flipped position without choosing between the logical amplitudes.

Identification is unique only within {I,X1,X2,X3}\{I,X_1,X_2,X_3\}{I,X1​,X2​,X3​}. The error X1X3X_1X_3X1​X3​ shares X2X_2X2​'s syndrome. Applying X2X_2X2​ then flips all three bits, causing the logical bit flip counted in §1.1.

∣ψL⟩=32∣000⟩+i2∣111⟩,X2∣ψL⟩=32∣010⟩+i2∣101⟩,∣after parity extraction⟩=(32∣010⟩+i2∣101⟩)∣11⟩A,X2∣data after measurement⟩=32∣000⟩+i2∣111⟩.\begin{aligned} |\psi_L\rangle&=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}|000\rangle+\frac i2|111\rangle,\\ X_2|\psi_L\rangle&=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}|010\rangle+\frac i2|101\rangle,\\ |\text{after parity extraction}\rangle &=\left(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}|010\rangle+\frac i2|101\rangle\right)|11\rangle_A,\\ X_2|\text{data after measurement}\rangle &=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}|000\rangle+\frac i2|111\rangle. \end{aligned}∣ψL​⟩X2​∣ψL​⟩∣after parity extraction⟩X2​∣data after measurement⟩​=23​​∣000⟩+2i​∣111⟩,=23​​∣010⟩+2i​∣101⟩,=(23​​∣010⟩+2i​∣101⟩)∣11⟩A​,=23​​∣000⟩+2i​∣111⟩.​

Decode the sign pattern

With S1=Z1Z2S_1=Z_1Z_2S1​=Z1​Z2​, S2=Z2Z3S_2=Z_2Z_3S2​=Z2​Z3​ and at most one XXX error, which error has syndrome (1,1)(1,1)(1,1)?

Your answer

What can one physical qubit reveal?

Measure qubit 1 of α∣000⟩+β∣111⟩\alpha|000\rangle+\beta|111\rangleα∣000⟩+β∣111⟩ in the ZZZ basis. What does a single outcome tell you about the input amplitude α\alphaα?

Zero occurs with probability ∣α∣2|\alpha|^2∣α∣2. Estimating that probability requires repeated, identically prepared inputs. Before measurement, the relative phase is stored in joint correlations, although measurements on one qubit alone cannot reveal it, Eq. (1.11). Measuring a data qubit in ZZZ measures the logical value and destroys that coherence.

Your prediction

What can measurements on one physical qubit tell us? Its reduced density operator, ρ1\rho_1ρ1​, reproduces every measurement probability available on qubit 1 alone.

We obtain it by tracing out qubits 2 and 3, written Tr⁡23\operatorname{Tr}_{23}Tr23​: we sum over their unobserved basis labels. Each physical qubit retains the logical populations but has no off-diagonal coherence. For qubit 1,

ρ1=Tr⁡23(∣ψL⟩⟨ψL∣)=∣α∣2∣0⟩⟨0∣+∣β∣2∣1⟩⟨1∣.\rho_1=\operatorname{Tr}_{23}(|\psi_L\rangle\langle\psi_L|) =|\alpha|^2|0\rangle\langle0|+|\beta|^2|1\rangle\langle1|.ρ1​=Tr23​(∣ψL​⟩⟨ψL​∣)=∣α∣2∣0⟩⟨0∣+∣β∣2∣1⟩⟨1∣.
(1.11)
Derivation · Carry out the partial trace

Start from the joint density operator, retaining both off-diagonal terms:

ρ=∣α∣2∣000⟩⟨000∣+αβ∗∣000⟩⟨111∣+βα∗∣111⟩⟨000∣+∣β∣2∣111⟩⟨111∣.\rho=|\alpha|^2|000\rangle\langle000|+\alpha\beta^*|000\rangle\langle111| +\beta\alpha^*|111\rangle\langle000|+|\beta|^2|111\rangle\langle111|.ρ=∣α∣2∣000⟩⟨000∣+αβ∗∣000⟩⟨111∣+βα∗∣111⟩⟨000∣+∣β∣2∣111⟩⟨111∣.

The partial trace of a product operator is Tr⁡23(∣a⟩⟨b∣⊗∣u⟩⟨v∣)=∣a⟩⟨b∣⟨v∣u⟩\operatorname{Tr}_{23}(|a\rangle\langle b|\otimes|u\rangle\langle v|)=|a\rangle\langle b|\langle v|u\rangleTr23​(∣a⟩⟨b∣⊗∣u⟩⟨v∣)=∣a⟩⟨b∣⟨v∣u⟩. Apply it to each term:

ρ1=∣α∣2∣0⟩⟨0∣⟨00∣00⟩+αβ∗∣0⟩⟨1∣⟨11∣00⟩+βα∗∣1⟩⟨0∣⟨00∣11⟩+∣β∣2∣1⟩⟨1∣⟨11∣11⟩=∣α∣2∣0⟩⟨0∣+∣β∣2∣1⟩⟨1∣.\begin{aligned} \rho_1={}&|\alpha|^2|0\rangle\langle0|\langle00|00\rangle +\alpha\beta^*|0\rangle\langle1|\langle11|00\rangle\\ &+\beta\alpha^*|1\rangle\langle0|\langle00|11\rangle +|\beta|^2|1\rangle\langle1|\langle11|11\rangle\\ ={}&|\alpha|^2|0\rangle\langle0|+|\beta|^2|1\rangle\langle1|. \end{aligned}ρ1​==​∣α∣2∣0⟩⟨0∣⟨00∣00⟩+αβ∗∣0⟩⟨1∣⟨11∣00⟩+βα∗∣1⟩⟨0∣⟨00∣11⟩+∣β∣2∣1⟩⟨1∣⟨11∣11⟩∣α∣2∣0⟩⟨0∣+∣β∣2∣1⟩⟨1∣.​

Orthogonality of 000000 and 111111 removes the cross terms, so this is not a clone of the input. By symmetry, qubits 2 and 3 have the same reduced state. The populations are nonnegative and sum to one; basis inputs remain pure. Phase survives in joint correlations.

A logical Pauli acts on the encoded qubit as an ordinary Pauli acts on one qubit.

Several physical operators can have the same action on the code. Choosing a representative means choosing one physical implementation. We use

Xˉ≡X1X2X3,Zˉ≡Z1.\bar X\equiv X_1X_2X_3,\qquad \bar Z\equiv Z_1.Xˉ≡X1​X2​X3​,Zˉ≡Z1​.
(1.12)Definition

Xˉ\bar XXˉ exchanges the code states; Zˉ\bar ZZˉ changes their relative sign. Since the checks act as identity on the code, Z1≡Z2≡Z3Z_1\equiv Z_2\equiv Z_3Z1​≡Z2​≡Z3​ there. Both logical operators commute with the checks:

[Si,Xˉ]=[Si,Zˉ]=0,i=1,2.[S_i,\bar X]=[S_i,\bar Z]=0,\qquad i=1,2.[Si​,Xˉ]=[Si​,Zˉ]=0,i=1,2.
(1.13)
Derivation · Even sign changes and logical information

Count minus signs in the commutator [A,B]=AB−BA[A,B]=AB-BA[A,B]=AB−BA. Each stabilizer meets two factors of Xˉ\bar XXˉ:

(Z1Z2)(X1X2X3)=(−1)2(X1X2X3)(Z1Z2),(Z2Z3)(X1X2X3)=(−1)2(X1X2X3)(Z2Z3).\begin{aligned} (Z_1Z_2)(X_1X_2X_3)&=(-1)^2(X_1X_2X_3)(Z_1Z_2),\\ (Z_2Z_3)(X_1X_2X_3)&=(-1)^2(X_1X_2X_3)(Z_2Z_3). \end{aligned}(Z1​Z2​)(X1​X2​X3​)(Z2​Z3​)(X1​X2​X3​)​=(−1)2(X1​X2​X3​)(Z1​Z2​),=(−1)2(X1​X2​X3​)(Z2​Z3​).​

Products of ZZZ operators commute with Z1Z_1Z1​, so all four commutators vanish. The logical actions are

Xˉ(α∣000⟩+β∣111⟩)=β∣000⟩+α∣111⟩,Zˉ(α∣000⟩+β∣111⟩)=α∣000⟩−β∣111⟩.\begin{aligned} \bar X(\alpha|000\rangle+\beta|111\rangle)&=\beta|000\rangle+\alpha|111\rangle,\\ \bar Z(\alpha|000\rangle+\beta|111\rangle)&=\alpha|000\rangle-\beta|111\rangle. \end{aligned}Xˉ(α∣000⟩+β∣111⟩)Zˉ(α∣000⟩+β∣111⟩)​=β∣000⟩+α∣111⟩,=α∣000⟩−β∣111⟩.​

Both outputs remain in the joint +1+1+1 eigenspace. For basis bits a,b∈{0,1}a,b\in\{0,1\}a,b∈{0,1}, a⊕ba\oplus ba⊕b is their sum modulo two, also called XOR. It is zero when they agree and one when they differ. Parity extraction writes this bit onto a blank ancilla:

∣a,b⟩∣0⟩A⟼∣a,b⟩∣a⊕b⟩A.|a,b\rangle|0\rangle_A\longmapsto|a,b\rangle|a\oplus b\rangle_A.∣a,b⟩∣0⟩A​⟼∣a,b⟩∣a⊕b⟩A​.

Clean components both write zero, leaving ∣ψL⟩∣00⟩A|\psi_L\rangle|00\rangle_A∣ψL​⟩∣00⟩A​ unchanged. After XkX_kXk​, both write syndrome sks_ksk​, giving Xk∣ψL⟩∣sk⟩AX_k|\psi_L\rangle|s_k\rangle_AXk​∣ψL​⟩∣sk​⟩A​. Norm is preserved. The ancillas learn the syndrome without distinguishing the logical components or their amplitudes.

Commutation alone does not protect the state: measuring Zˉ\bar ZZˉ also commutes with the checks, but reveals the logical value. Parity preserves the superposition because both logical components give the same record.

This code corrects one XXX error at an unknown location. The weight of a Pauli product counts the qubits on which it acts nontrivially. Thus X1X2X3X_1X_2X_3X1​X2​X3​ has weight three, while Z1Z_1Z1​ has weight one.

Write a code's parameters as [[n,k,d]][[n,k,d]][[n,k,d]]:

Parameter Meaning
nnn Number of data qubits.
kkk Number of encoded logical qubits.
ddd Minimum weight of an allowed Pauli error that changes the logical state without changing the syndrome.

This code is [[3,1,3]][[3,1,3]][[3,1,3]] against bit flips only: its smallest nontrivial undetectable XXX operator is Xˉ=X1X2X3\bar X=X_1X_2X_3Xˉ=X1​X2​X3​. Against general errors its distance is one because Z1=ZˉZ_1=\bar ZZ1​=Zˉ has no syndrome. Measurement ancillas add hardware but do not count toward nnn.

Original source ↗

Preskill develops the bit-flip checks and ancilla extraction while constructing Shor's code, which also protects phase. Collective parity measurement preserves a logical superposition that separate value measurements would collapse.

You can now locate and undo a single XXX error without measuring the logical value. Next, apply these checks to a coherent rotation.

§

1.4 · Discretization: how measurement turns a continuum into a coin flip

A rotation on one physical qubit combines clean and XXX-flipped states. They give different parity outcomes. Measurement selects one part and tells us which correction to apply, whatever the angle.

Let only qubit 2 undergo the rotation in Eq. (1.7):

RX(2)(θ)∣ψL⟩=cos⁡(θ/2)∣ψL⟩−isin⁡(θ/2)X2∣ψL⟩.R_X^{(2)}(\theta)|\psi_L\rangle =\cos(\theta/2)|\psi_L\rangle-i\sin(\theta/2)X_2|\psi_L\rangle.RX(2)​(θ)∣ψL​⟩=cos(θ/2)∣ψL​⟩−isin(θ/2)X2​∣ψL​⟩.
(1.14)
Derivation · Apply the rotation to the encoded amplitudes

Apply the rotation to each encoded component. Write c=cos⁡(θ/2)c=\cos(\theta/2)c=cos(θ/2) and u=sin⁡(θ/2)u=\sin(\theta/2)u=sin(θ/2), both real, and tensor the rotation with identity on the other qubits:

(I⊗RX⊗I)(α∣000⟩+β∣111⟩)=cα∣000⟩+cβ∣111⟩−iuα∣010⟩−iuβ∣101⟩=c∣ψL⟩−iuX2∣ψL⟩.\begin{aligned} (I\otimes R_X\otimes I)(\alpha|000\rangle+\beta|111\rangle) &=c\alpha|000\rangle+c\beta|111\rangle-iu\alpha|010\rangle-iu\beta|101\rangle\\ &=c|\psi_L\rangle-iuX_2|\psi_L\rangle. \end{aligned}(I⊗RX​⊗I)(α∣000⟩+β∣111⟩)​=cα∣000⟩+cβ∣111⟩−iuα∣010⟩−iuβ∣101⟩=c∣ψL​⟩−iuX2​∣ψL​⟩.​

The clean state occupies 000000000 and 111111111; the flipped state occupies 010010010 and 101101101. These sectors are orthogonal and individually normalized, so the rotated state has squared norm c2+u2=1c^2+u^2=1c2+u2=1. Zero angle leaves only the clean sector; π\piπ leaves only the flipped sector. Intermediate angles give a coherent superposition, not a classical mixture.

Ideal parity extraction attaches ancilla record 000000 to the clean component and 111111 to the X2X_2X2​ component. Measuring the ancillas selects one component while preserving its logical amplitudes. Correct the flagged component with another X2X_2X2​.

An outcome s=(s1,s2)s=(s_1,s_2)s=(s1​,s2​) occurs with probability P(s)P(s)P(s).

The normalized data state conditioned on that outcome is ∣ψs⟩|\psi_s\rangle∣ψs​⟩. It exists only when the outcome has nonzero probability.

Fidelity measures how closely the output matches the encoded input: F=∣⟨ψL∣ψout⟩∣2F=|\langle\psi_L|\psi_{\rm out}\rangle|^2F=∣⟨ψL​∣ψout​⟩∣2, where ∣ψout⟩|\psi_{\rm out}\rangle∣ψout​⟩ is the output data state. Fidelity one means the states agree up to global phase.

Use III in the clean branch and X2X_2X2​ in the flagged branch. Since X22=IX_2^2=IX22​=I, the flagged output is −i(u/∣u∣)∣ψL⟩-i(u/|u|)|\psi_L\rangle−i(u/∣u∣)∣ψL​⟩. Each corrected overlap has magnitude one, so F=∣⟨ψL∣ψout⟩∣2=1F=|\langle\psi_L|\psi_{\rm out}\rangle|^2=1F=∣⟨ψL​∣ψout​⟩∣2=1. Negative ccc or uuu changes only a global phase. The result holds for every real angle. A zero-probability branch has no conditional state to normalize.

The probabilities sum to one. Either possible outcome preserves the encoded amplitudes.

This resolves the continuum puzzle. The angle sets the outcome probabilities, independently of α\alphaα and β\betaβ. Both branches preserve those amplitudes. Each has a known correction, so recovery never needs to estimate the angle.

An unencoded qubit generally changes under the same rotation. Write ⟨X⟩=⟨ψ∣X∣ψ⟩\langle X\rangle=\langle\psi|X|\psi\rangle⟨X⟩=⟨ψ∣X∣ψ⟩ for its input expectation. Its fidelity is the squared overlap with that input:

Fbare=1−sin⁡2(θ/2)(1−⟨X⟩2).F_{\rm bare}=1-\sin^2(\theta/2)\bigl(1-\langle X\rangle^2\bigr).Fbare​=1−sin2(θ/2)(1−⟨X⟩2).
(1.16)
Derivation · Compute the unprotected overlap

Square the overlap with the input, writing c=cos⁡(θ/2)c=\cos(\theta/2)c=cos(θ/2) and u=sin⁡(θ/2)u=\sin(\theta/2)u=sin(θ/2). Hermiticity makes x=⟨X⟩x=\langle X\ranglex=⟨X⟩ real, with −1≤x≤1-1\leq x\leq1−1≤x≤1:

⟨ψ∣RX∣ψ⟩=c−iux,∣c−iux∣2=(c−iux)(c+iux)=c2+u2x2=1−u2(1−x2).\langle\psi|R_X|\psi\rangle=c-iux,\qquad |c-iux|^2=(c-iux)(c+iux)=c^2+u^2x^2=1-u^2(1-x^2).⟨ψ∣RX​∣ψ⟩=c−iux,∣c−iux∣2=(c−iux)(c+iux)=c2+u2x2=1−u2(1−x2).

At x=0x=0x=0, the fidelity is c2c^2c2, its minimum over pure inputs at fixed angle. An XXX eigenstate has x2=1x^2=1x2=1 and fidelity one because the rotation changes only its global phase.

For an average over pure inputs uniformly distributed on the Bloch sphere, let x=⟨X⟩x=\langle X\ranglex=⟨X⟩, y=⟨Y⟩y=\langle Y\rangley=⟨Y⟩, and z=⟨Z⟩z=\langle Z\ranglez=⟨Z⟩. Pure states satisfy x2+y2+z2=1x^2+y^2+z^2=1x2+y2+z2=1. Rotational symmetry makes the averages of these three squared coordinates equal, so each is 1/31/31/3. Averaging the fidelity formula therefore gives ⟨Fbare⟩=1−23sin⁡2(θ/2)\langle F_{\rm bare}\rangle=1-\tfrac23\sin^2(\theta/2)⟨Fbare​⟩=1−32​sin2(θ/2). Zero angle gives fidelity one for every input. Thus the minimum fidelity differs from the state average.

Vary the rotation to change syndrome probabilities; vary the stored state to test preservation of arbitrary amplitudes. Choose that state with polar and azimuth: α=cos⁡(ϑ/2)\alpha=\cos(\vartheta/2)α=cos(ϑ/2) and β=eiφsin⁡(ϑ/2)\beta=e^{i\varphi}\sin(\vartheta/2)β=eiφsin(ϑ/2), with angles in radians. Only 000000000 and 111111111 have nonzero initial amplitudes. theta rotates the selected qubit; correct switches recovery on or off for the selected fidelities. Each calculation starts from this encoded state, with ideal measurement and recovery.

The first panel shows basis probabilities before correction. Conditional states are separately normalized, so rare branches can have tall stems. The second panel shows branch probabilities and FbareF_{\rm bare}Fbare​ versus rotation angle. Phases remain in the calculation. Reduced-state readouts describe the original encoded state.

Each branch has a fidelity FsF_sFs​. The ensemble fidelity averages these values with their outcome probabilities: Fensemble=∑sP(s)FsF_{\rm ensemble}=\sum_s P(s)F_sFensemble​=∑s​P(s)Fs​.

The readout labeled “Selected ensemble fidelity” follows the correction switch. “Corrected ensemble fidelity” always shows what ideal recovery would achieve, even when the switch is off. The default polar angle is 1.0471.0471.047 rad; preset angles use their displayed decimal values.

How often does a small rotation flag?

For θ=0.2\theta=0.2θ=0.2 rad on qubit 2 with ideal parity measurement, predict the probability of syndrome (1,1)(1,1)(1,1). Enter a probability. Compare 0.20.20.2 (probability equals angle) and zero (small rotations never flag) with the Born rule.

The probability is sin⁡2(0.1)=0.009966711079379184…\sin^2(0.1)=0.009966711079379184\ldotssin2(0.1)=0.009966711079379184…. The amplitude is linear at small angle; the Born rule squares it in Eq. (1.15). A rare flag selects a full, correctable X2X_2X2​ error.

Try and check both branch weights. Turn correction off and watch “Selected ensemble fidelity” and the selected flagged-branch fidelity. The clean branch still matches the target; the flagged branch is orthogonal to it, so the selected ensemble fidelity equals the clean-branch probability.

Compare with . The latter uses 3.14163.14163.1416 rad, leaving a tiny clean probability; exact π\piπ would make it zero.

At , the bare qubit is nearly an XXX eigenstate, so its fidelity remains nearly one even though the encoded state can produce a flag. Change the target qubit and check the syndrome table.

Finally, vary the logical phase and rotation angle. Explain from the projectors why corrected fidelity stays one, and name an excluded error that could lower it.

Method: Store eight complex amplitude pairs. Acting on qubit k pairs indices differing in bit 3-k and evaluates c times the old amplitude minus i s times its partner. Compute each basis state's two Z-parities, project onto each accessible syndrome, sum squared amplitudes for the Born weight, and normalize nonzero branches. Correction permutes the flagged branch amplitudes with X_k. Fidelities use an explicit complex inner product. Partial trace sums products over the four configurations of qubits 2 and 3. The angle panel uses 201 samples on [0,pi].

Tolerances: Norms, branch probabilities, stabilizer expectations, partial traces, and corrected fidelities are checked to 1e-12 against independent matrix or Bloch-vector results. Exactly zero branch weights return no conditional state; nonzero rare branches are normalized without a probability cutoff. At the exact numeric value Math.PI the rotation uses c=0,s=1 to remove trigonometric endpoint roundoff. Fidelity readouts use 12 significant digits, displaying corrected fidelity as 1.

Display conventions

  • All outputs are computed from the stated model; preset states and angles are illustrative. Complex phases are retained in the model, although stems show only squared magnitudes.
  • Rotated, clean, and flagged stems are offset by -0.15, 0, and +0.15 basis-index units for visibility; the underlying basis indices remain integers. Labels and dashes distinguish the series.
  • The correction toggle changes selected fidelity readouts. Stems always show post-rotation and post-measurement states before correction; impossible conditional states are omitted and labeled.
  • The angle range labels denote intended multiples of π\piπ; numeric endpoints are rounded to four significant digits (3.142 and 6.283), and the default polar angle is 1.047 rad. The model evaluates numeric angles literally, without snapping them to π\piπ or π/3\pi/3π/3. Presets retain the specified 1.5708 and 3.1416 rad, so Full flip can retain a tiny clean probability. Exact θ=π\theta=\piθ=π is handled exactly.
  • The reduced state shown is the original encoded state, not the rotated state. Rotating physical qubit 1 can produce coherence in its reduced state before measurement.

Model limits

One coherent XXX-axis error on a single chosen qubit only; no simultaneous two-qubit errors or generic noise channel is modeled.

Both parity measurements and the syndrome-conditioned correction are perfect; no gate or measurement noise is included.

The bit-flip code cannot detect ZZZ errors, which can change the logical state without changing these syndromes. It has distance 1 against general errors.

Global phase is ignored in fidelity; relative phases remain part of the complex state vector. Basis probabilities alone do not specify that vector.

Branch probabilities are exact Born weights, not a sampled measurement record. Corrected fidelity 1 is a consequence of this restricted error model.

What remains after a clean outcome?

A single qubit of the bit-flip code undergoes RX(θ)R_X(\theta)RX​(θ), and ideal syndrome measurement reports (0,0)(0,0)(0,0) with nonzero probability. Which normalized state remains?

Your answer

For E=(abcd)E=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{smallmatrix}\right)E=(ac​bd​), the entries also check the sign of YYY:

(e0,e1,e2,e3)=(a+d2,b+c2,c−b2i,a−d2),∑jejPj=(e0+e3e1−ie2e1+ie2e0−e3)=(abcd).(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)=\left(\frac{a+d}{2},\frac{b+c}{2},\frac{c-b}{2i},\frac{a-d}{2}\right),\qquad \sum_je_jP_j=\begin{pmatrix}e_0+e_3&e_1-ie_2\\e_1+ie_2&e_0-e_3\end{pmatrix} =\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}.(e0​,e1​,e2​,e3​)=(2a+d​,2b+c​,2ic−b​,2a−d​),j∑​ej​Pj​=(e0​+e3​e1​+ie2​​e1​−ie2​e0​−e3​​)=(ac​bd​).

For E=IE=IE=I only e0e_0e0​ survives; the rotation has (e0,e1,e2,e3)=(cos⁡(θ/2),−isin⁡(θ/2),0,0)(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)=(\cos(\theta/2),-i\sin(\theta/2),0,0)(e0​,e1​,e2​,e3​)=(cos(θ/2),−isin(θ/2),0,0). A finite operator basis represents the full continuum of errors without an angle grid.

If the same recovery corrects each of I,X,Y,ZI,X,Y,ZI,X,Y,Z exactly for every encoded state, it also corrects their linear combinations, including the operator components of a noise channel. Finite tests or separate error-dependent recoveries do not establish this. Module 2 gives the Knill–Laflamme conditions. Here we have proved recovery for the span of III and XkX_kXk​ at the chosen site; ZZZ errors remain unprotected.

For one rotated qubit, a clean syndrome leaves no residual rotation. That conclusion changes when all three qubits rotate by the same small angle: the clean branch retains a logical rotation of third order in that angle. Module 2 derives this case.

Theory of quantum error-correcting codes · further · PDF pp. 12–14, Theorems 3.1–3.2

Emanuel Knill and Raymond Laflamme · 1997 · Physical Review A · vol. 55 · pp. 34

Original source ↗ · DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevA.55.900

Theorem 3.1 shows why errors corrected by one common recovery remain correctable under linear combinations. Theorem 3.2 gives the general recovery criterion. Our proof here covers the clean component and a single-site XXX component.

Return to scaling and suppression.

You can now recover an arbitrary-angle XXX rotation on one physical qubit using ideal parity measurement and recovery. Next we ask how failure rates change as a code grows.

§

1.5 · Scaling, Λ, and what Google measured

A larger memory helps if it preserves the stored state more reliably. At each distance, Google varies the number of correction cycles and compares the decoded final value with the prepared value. A decay fit gives the logical error per cycle, εd\varepsilon_dεd​.

The suppression ratio Λ\LambdaΛ measures the improvement when distance increases by two. Values above one mean the larger code helps.

To relate that ratio to physical noise, Google uses an approximate scaling model for its surface code. A specified model of physical faults supplies an error probability ppp.

Its threshold pthp_{\rm th}pth​ is the noise level below which increasing distance suppresses logical failure.

The factor AAA sets the overall rate. The model uses common values of AAA and pthp_{\rm th}pth​ across the distances being compared:

εd≈A(ppth)(d+1)/2,Λ(d)≡εdεd+2.\varepsilon_d\approx A\left(\frac p{p_{\rm th}}\right)^{(d+1)/2},\qquad \Lambda(d)\equiv\frac{\varepsilon_d}{\varepsilon_{d+2}}.εd​≈A(pth​p​)(d+1)/2,Λ(d)≡εd+2​εd​​.
(1.18)Definition

Google uses this scaling form in Eq. (1) Quantum error correction below the surface code threshold, PDF p. 1 Original source ↗ · DOI: 10.1038/s41586-024-08449-y. Increasing ddd by two raises the exponent by one. The common factor AAA cancels in the ratio. The remaining factor is Λ≈pth/p\Lambda\approx p_{\rm th}/pΛ≈pth​/p within this model. The physical faults in the experiment include more than the independent data flips of our repetition model.

Google reports these surface-code rates for its 105-qubit processor using a neural-network decoder, a classical algorithm that interprets the measurement record. A suppression ratio describes improvement at one operating point. A threshold describes how that improvement changes with noise. How are the two related? For a surface code we cannot yet compute either, so we test the connection on the one code whose logical error we can write down exactly: the repetition code of §1.1, with independent bit flips, perfect readout and majority decoding. Everything in Eq. (1.19) and in the worked example after it is specific to that model. Only the definition of Λ\LambdaΛ, the fit form Eq. A positive floor makes the suppression ratio approach one. Failures do not cancel in this model, even when both occur.

A burst can cause faults on several qubits together, so adding distance need not make those faults as rare as an independent-flip model predicts.

Leakage means that a physical device leaves the two states used as ∣0⟩|0\rangle∣0⟩ and ∣1⟩|1\rangle∣1⟩.

Crosstalk means that an operation intended for one qubit also disturbs another. These mechanisms can weaken error suppression, but whether they produce a fixed floor depends on their behavior as the code grows.

In a separate experiment on the study's 72-qubit processor, Google ran repetition codes up to distance 29 with minimum-weight perfect matching decoding. Averaging the bit-flip and phase-flip experiments, the fit over distances 5–11 gave Λ=8.4±0.1\Lambda=8.4\pm0.1Λ=8.4±0.1 Quantum error correction below the surface code threshold, PDF pp. 4–5, Fig. 3a Original source ↗ · DOI: 10.1038/s41586-024-08449-y. An apparent floor lay near 10−1010^{-10}10−10 per cycle. Distance 29 recorded no errors, which does not establish zero probability. Rare damaging bursts occurred approximately once per hour, with no established origin Quantum error correction below the surface code threshold, PDF pp. 1, 4 Original source ↗ · DOI: 10.1038/s41586-024-08449-y. These observations depart from a single exponential curve; they do not establish the independent-failure model above.

Method: Accumulate log-binomial coefficients as sums of logarithms, form the first tail term with log1p(-p), advance adjacent terms by their exact ratio, and sum with log-sum-exp. Handle p=0, 1/2, and 1 explicitly. Evaluate the floor union as pL+(1-pL)floor to avoid subtracting nearly equal numbers. The first panel uses 201 equally spaced log10-p samples plus the exact crossing. Monte Carlo uses mulberry32 with seed (seed + d times 0x9E3779B9) modulo 2^32, one Bernoulli draw per bit per trial, and strict majority vote. Its plug-in standard error is sqrt(estimate(1-estimate)/N).

Tolerances: Independent dynamic-programming probabilities agree to 3e-13 relative error for displayed distances, including p=1e-4,d=15. No physical probability underflows in the control range. Log-probability ratios remain usable beyond that range even when exponentiation underflows. Monte Carlo checks use four binomial standard errors based on independent analytic probabilities, not the observed estimate.

Display conventions

  • Probabilities are computed, not measured. Preset choices are illustrative. Both probability plots use log10 values on linear axes, with a display floor of -16. Clipping never changes calculations or readouts; a clipped flat segment is not a modeled error floor.
  • Zero Monte Carlo estimates are drawn at -16 and identified in the legend. Their zero plug-in standard error is not an upper confidence bound; fewer than 10 observed failures trigger a warning.
  • The ladder connects only odd-distance values. For d=15d=15d=15, the exact Λ\LambdaΛ readout evaluates the additional distance 17 outside the ladder viewport.
  • The exact Λ\LambdaΛ readout always uses majority-vote rates without the floor; an additional readout shows the total-rate ratio when the floor is enabled.

Model limits

Code-capacity model only: data bit flips are independent across bits and rounds, with identical ppp. Correlated errors change the tail.

For equiprobable input bits and independent bit-flip noise, majority vote minimizes the average decoding error of this repetition code when p≤1/2p\le1/2p≤1/2 (all rules tie in average error at p=1/2p=1/2p=1/2); for known p>1/2p>1/2p>1/2, an optimal decoder reverses the majority. This lab intentionally keeps the majority rule fixed above threshold.

No syndrome-measurement errors, gate errors, leakage, reset errors, or circuit-level noise are included.

The floor is a phenomenological add-on with independent failure events. It does not simulate a correlated physical error process or cancellation of logical flips.

This distance protects against bit flips only. A repetition code of this form does not protect an arbitrary qubit against phase errors.

§

1.6 · When the measurement itself is wrong

A wrong parity report can make a decoder damage clean data. Repeating the checks helps distinguish a bad report from a persistent data error. In the phenomenological model, each data qubit flips independently with probability ppp per round, and each recorded syndrome bit is independently wrong with probability qqq.

For a clean three-qubit block, trusting one noisy round and applying the lookup table introduces a wrong correction with probability

Pwrong correction=2q(1−q)+q2=2q−q2=2q+O(q2).P_{\rm wrong\ correction}=2q(1-q)+q^2=2q-q^2=2q+O(q^2).Pwrong correction​=2q(1−q)+q2=2q−q2=2q+O(q2).
(1.21)
Derivation · Enumerate the four possible false records

Enumerate the possible reports for clean data, whose true syndrome is 000000. Corrupt each report independently:

Recorded syndrome Probability Applied operation on a clean state
000000 (1−q)2(1-q)^2(1−q)2 III
101010 q(1−q)q(1-q)q(1−q) X1X_1X1​
010101 (1−q)q(1-q)q(1−q)q X3X_3X3​
111111 q2q^2q2 X2X_2X2​

The probabilities sum to [(1−q)+q]2=1[(1-q)+q]^2=1[(1−q)+q]2=1. Every nonzero report triggers a flip: Pwrong correction=1−(1−q)2=2q−q2P_{\rm wrong\ correction}=1-(1-q)^2=2q-q^2Pwrong correction​=1−(1−q)2=2q−q2. Exactly one wrong report has probability 2q(1−q)2q(1-q)2q(1−q); two have probability q2q^2q2. At q=0q=0q=0, no wrong correction occurs.

A longer open chain has the same problem: one wrong check can mimic a data-error segment ending at a boundary. Some wrong corrections therefore remain first order in qqq. Distance alone cannot make an untrusted record reliable.

This is the probability of adding a spurious data flip to a clean block. It is not yet a logical failure: a later reliable round can correct that flip.

Now repeat checks without immediately correcting the data. Changed data parities persist until another fault or correction. An isolated wrong report lasts one recorded round. A detection event marks a change in a recorded check:

Di,t≡si,t⊕si,t−1.D_{i,t}\equiv s_{i,t}\oplus s_{i,t-1}.Di,t​≡si,t​⊕si,t−1​.
(1.22)Definition

Here si,ts_{i,t}si,t​ records check iii in round ttt, and ⊕\oplus⊕ is addition modulo two. Given the initial record, syndromes and events contain the same information. Our examples start from si,0=0s_{i,0}=0si,0​=0.

An isolated interior data flip changes two neighboring checks in the same round, producing a spatial pair. A boundary flip changes one check. A wrong report changes 0,0,00,0,00,0,0 into 0,1,00,1,00,1,0, producing events on entry and exit on the same check. The temporal pair requires observations on both sides of the wrong report. With several faults, different histories can share an event pattern.

Read a temporal pair

With repeated ideal parity extraction except for one isolated wrong recorded syndrome bit, away from the first and last round, which detection-event pattern signals that measurement error?

Your answer

The noise models add faults in stages: code capacity allows data faults; phenomenological noise adds wrong reports; a circuit-level model allows faults in individual gates, idles, resets, and measurements. One circuit fault can create correlated data and syndrome errors.

What the next decoder must decide

You can now distinguish isolated data and measurement faults by their signatures in a syndrome history. When faults overlap, several histories can explain the same record; Modules 6 and 7 in the Google-Willow roadmap examine how circuit faults arise and how a decoder chooses a recovery.

Rotate the code into the phase basis

Show why Z2Z_2Z2​ is invisible in the bit-flip code. Then use ∣±⟩=(∣0⟩±∣1⟩)/2|\pm\rangle=(|0\rangle\pm|1\rangle)/\sqrt2∣±⟩=(∣0⟩±∣1⟩)/2​ to encode against one ZZZ error. Give the logical basis states, stabilizers, complete single-error syndrome table, and corrections. State its phase-flip distance and a weight-one error it cannot correct.

Hint

Conjugate the entire bit-flip construction by H⊗3H^{\otimes3}H⊗3; HXH=ZHXH=ZHXH=Z and HZH=XHZH=XHZH=X.

  • Writes Z2∣ψL⟩=α∣000⟩−β∣111⟩Z_2|\psi_L\rangle=\alpha|000\rangle-\beta|111\rangleZ2​∣ψL​⟩=α∣000⟩−β∣111⟩ with unchanged syndrome 000000.

On the old code, Z2Z_2Z2​ changes only the sign of the 111111111 amplitude. It commutes with both old ZZZ checks, so the syndrome stays 000000. Now conjugate states and checks:

∣0L′⟩=H⊗3∣000⟩=∣+++⟩,∣1L′⟩=∣−−−⟩,S1′=X1X2,S2′=X2X3.|0_L'\rangle=H^{\otimes3}|000\rangle=|+++\rangle,\quad |1_L'\rangle=|---\rangle,\quad S_1'=X_1X_2,\quad S_2'=X_2X_3.∣0L′​⟩=H⊗3∣000⟩=∣+++⟩,∣1L′​⟩=∣−−−⟩,S1′​=X1​X2​,S2′​=X2​X3​.

Since X∣+⟩=∣+⟩X|+\rangle=|+\rangleX∣+⟩=∣+⟩ and X∣−⟩=−∣−⟩X|-\rangle=-|-\rangleX∣−⟩=−∣−⟩, both check products have eigenvalue +1+1+1 on both code states. A shared ZkZ_kZk​ anticommutes with the check's XkX_kXk​:

ES1′E relative signS2′E relative signsI+1+100Z1−1+110Z2−1−111Z3+1−101\begin{array}{c|cc|c} E&S_1' E\text{ relative sign}&S_2' E\text{ relative sign}&s\\\hline I&+1&+1&00\\ Z_1&-1&+1&10\\ Z_2&-1&-1&11\\ Z_3&+1&-1&01 \end{array}EIZ1​Z2​Z3​​S1′​E relative sign+1−1−1+1​S2′​E relative sign+1+1−1−1​s00101101​​

Apply ZkZ_kZk​ to each flagged branch: Zk2=IZ_k^2=IZk2​=I. The smallest undetectable nontrivial ZZZ product is Z1Z2Z3Z_1Z_2Z_3Z1​Z2​Z3​, which exchanges the codewords. The distance is three against phase flips only. Yet X1(α∣+++⟩+β∣−−−⟩)=α∣+++⟩−β∣−−−⟩X_1(\alpha|+++\rangle+\beta|---\rangle) =\alpha|+++\rangle-\beta|---\rangleX1​(α∣+++⟩+β∣−−−⟩)=α∣+++⟩−β∣−−−⟩ has syndrome zero, so general-error distance remains one. Hadamards exchange the protected error type; they do not protect both types at once.

Where does a floor take over?

Suppose a code has ε7=1.4×10−3\varepsilon_7=1.4\times10^{-3}ε7​=1.4×10−3 per cycle and constant Λ=2\Lambda=2Λ=2 for every two-distance increase. Add an independent failure floor 10−610^{-6}10−6 per cycle using Eq. (1.20). Define domination as the first odd distance where the correctable component is below the floor. Find that distance, the total rate there, and the best asymptotic rate.

Hint

Count two-distance increases from the given starting distance. Each increase divides the correctable rate by Λ\LambdaΛ. First compare that component with the floor, then use Eq. (1.20) to calculate the total.

Check against the rubric

  • Solves the logarithmic inequality and checks both neighboring odd distances.
  • Uses the union formula for the total and identifies a 10−610^{-6}10−6 asymptote rather than zero.
Show model solution

The crossover condition is

1.4×10−32k<10−6  ⟺  2k>1400  ⟺  k>ln⁡1400ln⁡2=10.451211….\frac{1.4\times10^{-3}}{2^k}<10^{-6} \iff 2^k>1400 \iff k>\frac{\ln1400}{\ln2}=10.451211\ldots.2k1.4×10−3​<10−6⟺2k>1400⟺k>ln2ln1400​=10.451211….

The first integer is k=11k=11k=11, giving d=29d=29d=29. At d=27d=27d=27, the correctable rate is 1.3671875×10−61.3671875\times10^{-6}1.3671875×10−6; at d=29d=29d=29, it is 6.8359375×10−76.8359375\times10^{-7}6.8359375×10−7. The total at d=29d=29d=29 is

6.8359375×10−7+10−6−(6.8359375×10−7)10−6=1.68359306640625×10−6.6.8359375\times10^{-7}+10^{-6}-(6.8359375\times10^{-7})10^{-6} =1.68359306640625\times10^{-6}.6.8359375×10−7+10−6−(6.8359375×10−7)10−6=1.68359306640625×10−6.

The total approaches 10−610^{-6}10−6 per cycle from above. Improvement continues beyond the crossover, but no finite distance reaches the asymptote.

Reconstruct the experimental ladder

Google's 2021 repetition experiment quotes measured rates 8.7×10−38.7\times10^{-3}8.7×10−3 per round with 5 total qubits and 6.7×10−56.7\times10^{-5}6.7×10−5 with 21 total qubits Exponential suppression of bit or phase errors with cyclic error correction, PDF p. 4 Original source ↗ · DOI: 10.1038/s41586-021-03588-y. There are ddd data and d−1d-1d−1 measure qubits. Convert the counts to distance, infer an effective constant Λ from the endpoints using Eq. (1.18), and compare it with the paper's fitted ΛX=3.18±0.08\Lambda_X=3.18\pm0.08ΛX​=3.18±0.08 and ΛZ=2.99±0.09\Lambda_Z=2.99\pm0.09ΛZ​=2.99±0.09 on that same page. Explain why neither the endpoint estimate nor the fits must equal this module's code-capacity 1/(4p)1/(4p)1/(4p).

Hint

First write the total qubit count as data plus measure qubits and solve for ddd. Then count the increases of two between the endpoint distances. If that count is rrr, a constant suppression factor gives εdlow/εdhigh=Λr\varepsilon_{d_{\rm low}}/\varepsilon_{d_{\rm high}}=\Lambda^rεdlow​​/εdhigh​​=Λr.

Check against the rubric
  • Converts total counts 5 and 21 to distances 3 and 11, hence four suppression steps.
  • Takes the fourth root of the rate ratio and reports approximately 3.38.
  • Distinguishes the endpoint estimate from fits using the full data, boundary exclusions, and code basis.
  • Names faulty circuits and decoding as differences from independent data flips with perfect checks.
Show model solution

The hardware count is 2d−12d-12d−1, so d=(ntotal+1)/2d=(n_{\rm total}+1)/2d=(ntotal​+1)/2: distances 3 and 11. There are (11−3)/2=4(11-3)/2=4(11−3)/2=4 rungs, and the common fit prefactor cancels:

ε3ε11=Λeff4,Λeff=(8.7×10−36.7×10−5)1/4=(129.850746…)1/4=3.37567877….\frac{\varepsilon_3}{\varepsilon_{11}}=\Lambda_{\rm eff}^{4},\qquad \Lambda_{\rm eff}=\left(\frac{8.7\times10^{-3}}{6.7\times10^{-5}}\right)^{1/4} =(129.850746\ldots)^{1/4}=3.37567877\ldots.ε11​ε3​​=Λeff4​,Λeff​=(6.7×10−58.7×10−3​)1/4=(129.850746…)1/4=3.37567877….

The endpoint estimate rounds to 3.38, roughly a factor of three per step. The endpoints are rounded; the paper fits distance data and excludes the case with three total qubits to reduce boundary effects. The XXX and ZZZ labels denote phase-flip and bit-flip codes, respectively, so these are distinct fits.

Comparison with 1/(4p)1/(4p)1/(4p) needs a physical-noise model. Gates, idle decoherence during measurement, readout, reset, and decoding all contribute Exponential suppression of bit or phase errors with cyclic error correction, PDF p. 5, Fig. 4 Original source ↗ · DOI: 10.1038/s41586-021-03588-y; the paper also discusses leakage and crosstalk Exponential suppression of bit or phase errors with cyclic error correction, PDF p. 4 Original source ↗ · DOI: 10.1038/s41586-021-03588-y. A component gate-error probability cannot supply the missing code-capacity ppp. Even ideal repetition has finite-distance and (1−p)(1-p)(1−p) corrections.

Let faults arrive in neighboring pairs

Majority voting counts flipped qubits. How many independent physical events produce those flips?

Keep the majority decoder and perfect checks, but change the physical model. Each data qubit has an independent XXX event of probability ppp. Independently, each neighboring edge of an open chain has an XiXi+1X_iX_{i+1}Xi​Xi+1​ event of probability p2p_2p2​ per round. All events compose by XOR, so an overlapping flip can cancel. For d=3d=3d=3 and 555, find the leading failure terms as p,p2→0p,p_2\to0p,p2​→0. Include the pure-independent term and the leading mixed term for d=5d=5d=5. What exponent results if p2p_2p2​ is of the same order as ppp? Distinguish Pauli-weight distance from the number of fault events needed to make a logical operator, and say what an improved decoder can and cannot fix.

Hint

One pair defeats a three-bit majority. For five bits, a pair plus a single outside it has weight three; two disjoint pairs have weight four, while overlapping pairs cancel their common bit.

Check against the rubric
  • Specifies the independent-per-edge model and composes overlapping flips by XOR.
  • Counts two single-pair failures for d=3d=3d=3 and retains the independent 3p23p^23p2 term.
  • Counts 12 pair-plus-outside-single and three disjoint-pair patterns for d=5d=5d=5, alongside 10p310p^310p3.
  • Explains the exponent change when p2=cpp_2=cpp2​=cp for fixed c>0c>0c>0 and the recovery of the usual exponent when p2=O(p2)p_2=O(p^2)p2​=O(p2).
  • Separates unchanged Pauli-weight distance from event distance and explains the syndrome ambiguity.
Show model solution

For d=3d=3d=3, either edge event defeats the majority, contributing 2p22p_22p2​. Independent singles contribute 3p23p^23p2. Joint events and absent-fault probabilities correct higher terms:

pL(3)=2p2+3p2+O(pp2+p22+p3).p_L(3)=2p_2+3p^2+O(pp_2+p_2^2+p^3).pL​(3)=2p2​+3p2+O(pp2​+p22​+p3).

The 3p23p^23p2 term counts independent singles. When p2p_2p2​ scales with ppp, mixed terms also contribute at second order. For d=5d=5d=5, one pair is correctable. Four edges each have three outside sites: 4⋅3=124\cdot3=124⋅3=12 failing pair-plus-single patterns. Disjoint edge pairs (12,34)(12,34)(12,34), (12,45)(12,45)(12,45), and (23,45)(23,45)(23,45) also fail. Overlapping pairs leave weight two after XOR and succeed. Three independent singles contribute (53)=10\binom53=10(35​)=10:

pL(5)=12pp2+3p22+10p3+O(p2p2+pp22+p23+p4).p_L(5)=12pp_2+3p_2^2+10p^3+O(p^2p_2+pp_2^2+p_2^3+p^4).pL​(5)=12pp2​+3p22​+10p3+O(p2p2​+pp22​+p23​+p4).

Both probabilities must be small. If p2=cpp_2=cpp2​=cp for fixed c>0c>0c>0, failure starts at order ppp for d=3d=3d=3 and p2p^2p2 for d=5d=5d=5, instead of p2p^2p2 and p3p^3p3. If p2=O(p2)p_2=O(p^2)p2​=O(p2), the original powers return with modified coefficients.

Pauli-weight distance still counts flipped qubits: the smallest undetectable nontrivial XXX operator has weight ddd. Event distance counts elementary events forming that operator. The all-XXX logical requires ⌈d/2⌉\lceil d/2\rceil⌈d/2⌉ events: one pair and one single for d=3d=3d=3, or two disjoint pairs and one single for d=5d=5d=5. Event distances are two and three; Pauli-weight distances remain three and five against bit flips only. Majority failure can occur sooner: one pair defeats d=3d=3d=3.

Knowing p2p_2p2​ lets a decoder favor more probable histories and improve coefficients. But histories differing by the logical all-XXX have the same syndrome. For d=3d=3d=3, a pair and its complementary single are both first-order possibilities when p2=cpp_2=cpp2​=cp. For d=5d=5d=5, two disjoint pairs share a syndrome with the remaining single. Syndrome alone cannot distinguish these alternatives. Removing the ambiguity requires extra information or suppression of the correlated process. Phase errors remain outside this model.

You can now calculate when repetition helps, explain how parity measurements guide recovery of a single-qubit XXX rotation, and interpret suppression without confusing it with a threshold. The protection costs extra data qubits, measurement ancillas, and repeated correction cycles. Protecting phase and decoding unreliable measurements require a code that handles both error types and a recovery rule that uses the syndrome history.
